title: Communicating the Vision
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison examines the crucial and chronically underestimated task of communicating a school's vision — arguing that a vision that exists only in the leader's head, or only on paper, has not yet been communicated at all. The article identifies the core failure: leaders believe a vision is clear because they have lived with it extensively, but staff have not undergone the same thinking process and need active, repeated, varied communication to internalize it. Allison outlines practical strategies including storytelling with concrete examples, embedding the vision in operational structures (timetabling, CPD, meeting agendas), and returning to it consistently in one-to-ones and group settings. He distinguishes declarative communication — announcing the vision — from embodied communication, arguing that the leader's own behavior is the most powerful medium: what she praises, what she notices, and how she spends her time tells staff more about actual priorities than any document. The piece closes with the reminder that moral purpose must anchor the vision — leaders guided by genuine commitment to students communicate with a conviction that no messaging strategy can manufacture.
points: A vision exists in an organization only to the degree it has been communicated repeatedly, variously, and concretely — the leader's internal clarity does not transfer automatically to staff who have not undergone the same thinking process.

Stories and concrete examples are far more powerful than abstract vision statements; when leaders illustrate the vision through real children and real classrooms it becomes tangible and motivating rather than rhetorical.

The leader's own behavior is the primary communication medium: what the headteacher praises, what she notices, and how she spends her time tells staff more about actual organizational priorities than any formal statement.

Making the vision structurally visible — embedding it in CPD, timetabling decisions, resource allocation, and meeting agendas — ensures it is not merely declared but demonstrated through the school's operating logic.

A strong moral purpose functions as the backbone of authentic communication: leaders who are genuinely guided by students' futures communicate with a conviction that managed messaging cannot replicate, and staff sense the difference.
quotes: One of the great privileges of being a Headteacher is seeing passionate professionals articulate what drives them every day. At a recent Middle Leader Development Programme, our Library Manager, Viv DaCosta and Head of Art, Steve Bloomer, delivered presentations on Communicating the Vision to aspiring middle leaders. Although their disciplines are very different, the messages at the heart of their talks were remarkably similar.

Vision alone is not enough. People rarely buy into a plan because of a spreadsheet or a strategic document. They buy into it because of the belief and enthusiasm of the person leading it.

Passion is contagious. It inspires colleagues to care more deeply, encourages pupils to engage more fully and creates momentum when challenges arise. The most influential leaders are often those who remind others why the work is worth doing.
This mindset is not driven by criticism of current practice but by a commitment to growth. Excellence is viewed not as a final destination but as an ongoing journey.
